1776-04-30.summary: Dumas reports opening himself to a French minister at The Hague, the request for French mediation or a Bourbon alliance, and the minister's fear that reconciled colonies would turn on their helpers. Printed decoded in the Franklin Papers 22:403-412.
1776-04-30.en: "... and that one must except from this number the holders of English public funds, and those European courts that have an understanding with the court of England. Far from helping you, they would sacrifice you to their interests or to their fear. The allies who suit you in this situation are France and Spain, for it is in their interest that you be free and independent of England, whose enormous sea power alarms them. I have therefore opened myself to a minister of France, and the copy and translation of your requests and of the letter of credence concerning me have been for at least a fortnight in the hands of the ministry, and so of the King of France. In my conversation with this minister I was able to see that the wishes of his nation are for you. He raised only one difficulty against the help that might be given to the colonies:

1776-05-14.summary: The French minister's answer of 21 May 1776: no mediation while the colonies are the King of England's subjects and no alliance while France is at peace, but Americans may buy arms and munitions in France as merchandise; Hortalez will apply to the Committee. Printed decoded in the Franklin Papers 22:433-436.
1776-05-14.en: 10 May reply: "May I anticipate you regarding the offer of expenses in all cases where your kindness would be useful to me? For a man such as you, by his knowledge, is not limited to a single kind of good offices." — "how one makes much of the servant for love of the master." — 21 May: "'You shall hear,' he said; 'you are clever, so you will understand me well. As to your first request, the King's mediation cannot take place as long as the colonies are subjects of the King of England, who besides would not accept it. As to your second request, the King is a true knight, his word is sacred to him; he has given it to the English to live in peace with them, and he will keep it. So as long as France is not at war with the English, he will not ally himself against them with the colonies, and will furnish no help to the latter.

1776-08-10.summary: The name Hortalez (spelled "Hortelez" in the numbers) and Dumas's plan to present himself also at the Spanish embassy; printed in Sparks 9 and Wharton 2.
1776-08-10.en: Image 41: "After long and careful thought, it seems to me that to answer their intention completely I ought to present myself also at the Spanish embassy, so as to be known there simply as charged with such a commission, [to open by that the ways of serving my principals ... and not incur the blame that might fall even on these gentlemen for having neglected] a power so worthy also of their confidence and of being sought out."

1776-09-01.summary: Hortalez; Deane's and Arthur Lee's letters on Prussia and on France; the advice to aim at correspondence with "le ministre même"; Madam V. Loder as forwarding address. Printed in Sparks, Wharton and (images 52-53) Force.
1776-09-01.en: 47: "This Hortalez of whom Mr. A. L., your friend, spoke to me ..." — 52: "Go on, he told me, ... and you will end by entering at last into correspondence with the minister himself." — 53: "I think I should not delay a moment in entrusting it to Madam V. Loder ..." (Dumas's forwarding address in The Hague, "chez Mad. V. Loder", Wharton vol. 2). — 51 is English.

1777-04-12.summary: Copies of letters from the French ministers at The Hague, the abbé Desnoyers and the duc de La Vauguyon; printed in Sparks 9:310-311.
1777-04-12.en: "You will find enclosed, Gentlemen, a copy of the letters which the ministers of France at The Hague, the abbé Desnoyers and the duc de la Vauguyon, have written to me. They will let you guess the contents of those I wrote to them ..."

1777-08-02.summary: The Courier du Bas-Rhin no longer writes to Dumas; he has made good openings for secret negotiations with people of the Amsterdam regency.
1777-08-02.en: "For some time the Courier du Bas-Rhin no longer writes to me. He still makes use, however, of what I send him ..." — "I have just made good openings for secret negotiations with people of the regency of Amsterdam. I will inform you, Gentlemen, of the outcome in due course."

1777-08-14.summary: Dumas wrote to the French ambassador at The Hague and travelled with the wife of Van Berckel, Pensionary of Amsterdam; the clear original to Franklin is printed in the Franklin Papers 24:428-434.
1777-08-14.en: "I had written to the ambassador of France at The Hague, on 2 August, a rather interesting letter ..." — "I had told him that I had made such good use of a journey with the wife of Mr. Van Berckel, Pensionary of Amsterdam, that I was sure of being well received by the husband ..."

1777-09-25.summary: "Le paquet, L, est dans le vaisseau pris": Dumas's packet L was in the captured ship. Bare in both copies.

1777-10-14.summary: "Le paquet, L, est dans le vaisseau pris": Dumas's packet L was in the captured ship. Bare in both copies.

1777-11-04.summary: Dumas had the piece put into the Mercure and the "Lettre hollandoise" published; he has the whole enemy cabal against him but is the Committee's.
1777-11-04.en:
"... Their party in this country keeps losing ground, even among persons of distinction. — It is your servant who had the piece put into the Mercure and published the Dutch letter, etc. I still have the whole enemy cabal here on my back. But I am yours. That reassures and consoles me. God save and bless united America ..."
(The "Lettre hollandoise" is the "Lettre Hollandoise d'un Négociant de — à son Correspondant ... sur le Crédit public de la Gr. Br. & de l'Amérique unie" enclosed with T, image 114.)

1777-11-28.summary: Through the Cleves gazetteer a memorial on Emden is to reach Frederick II; the King wants a navy; Arthur Lee has gone to Berlin; American privateers should bring prizes into Emden.
1777-11-28.en:
"Second extracts of my correspondence with the Courier du Bas-Rhin. From the first letters he wrote me I had reason to suspect that he passed mine on, whole or in extracts, directly or indirectly, to a certain Court. ... He answered me last month as follows: 'Your project, on Emden, pleased me very much ... I will make a memorial of all this, which I will have delivered into the King's own hands through persons who approach him every day and with whom I am in touch. I know that he has the strongest wish to found a navy; that is what all his aims tend to today.'"
"Meanwhile I had learned from our gentlemen that Mr. Lee had gone to Berlin." ... "He is quite right to want to found a navy; that alone is lacking to complete his power ... Let American privateers be free to enter Emden, for example, to bring in and sell their prizes there ..." ...

1778-02-24.summary: Dumas can procure the despatches of the Republic's ministers abroad and sends extracts to the Commissioners; an Amsterdam house has opened a subscription for four ships to trade directly with America.
1778-02-24.en: "I will only tell you that I have found means to procure the despatches of the ministers of the Republic at the courts of Europe, and that I send extracts of them regularly to your honourable Commission Plenipotentiary in Europe. ... I have preached so much to friends in a certain town that at last I have seen them take up again the boldness of their ancestors. A Dutch house at Amsterdam has opened a subscription of ten thousand pieces to send four ships, loaded with first necessities, to trade directly with your continent. Three thousand pieces are already subscribed. At their request I have written to the honourable Commission to ask for lists for the cargoes, and other directions."

1778-04-27.summary: Letters asked for from Paris have had their effect; one more is expected "pour frapper un grand coup".
1778-04-27.en: "I have received from Paris letters such as I had asked for; they have already had all the effect I expected of them; and I am expecting one more, to strike a great blow. If God blesses these measures, which are well concerted, I shall be able to announce good news to you next month."

1778-06-14.summary: Dumas's work is to cement the party formed to ruin English influence and detach the Republic from America's enemies; "Amsterdam, Harlem, Dort & Delft sont pour nous" ("sont" rests on a marked emendation).
1778-06-14.en: "I will say only in general what they [my operations] consist of: to cement and strengthen the party formed some time ago to ruin English influence here, to detach this Republic from your enemies, and to reconcile it to you and your friends. Amsterdam, Haarlem, Dort and Delft are for us."

1778-07-31.summary: The key to the blanks of the printed Dumas-Van Berckel letters: the Pensionary of Amsterdam, The Hague, the Grand Pensionary, Amsterdam, Their High Mightinesses, E. F. Van Berchel.
1778-07-31.en:
"There, Gentlemen, is a true Liberty-Tree man. Here are the names left blank in these letters: — the Pensionary of Amsterdam — The Hague — the Grand Pensionary — Amsterdam — Their High Mightinesses — E. F. van Berckel."
(Dumas spells "Berchel": no k in the key, and he uses c for k.)

1778-08-17.summary: The addressee's office in cipher; the letter is printed with Van Berckel named.
1778-08-17.en: "Duplicate of the copy of my letter of 17 August to the Pensionary of Amsterdam."

1779-05.summary: Run 1 (a cabal of Genevan and Swiss bankers) is printed. Not printed: the friends' unanimous voice that J. de Neufville & fils alone deserve the Committee's confidence at Amsterdam, the previous houses "faux amis"; "On trompe l'ambassadeur de F="; and the name "J. de Neufville & fils" in the two English letters.

1779-05-after17.summary: Run 1 (a cabal of Genevan and Swiss bankers) is printed. Not printed: the friends' unanimous voice that J. de Neufville & fils alone deserve the Committee's confidence at Amsterdam, the previous houses "faux amis"; "On trompe l'ambassadeur de F="; and the name "J. de Neufville & fils" in the two English letters.

1779-06-21.summary: Run 1 (a cabal of Genevan and Swiss bankers) is printed. Not printed: the friends' unanimous voice that J. de Neufville & fils alone deserve the Committee's confidence at Amsterdam, the previous houses "faux amis"; "On trompe l'ambassadeur de F="; and the name "J. de Neufville & fils" in the two English letters.

1779-09-20.summary: Dumas is to leave for the Texel with letters and secret instructions for John Paul Jones's squadron; the numbers spell "csmmodore jones e his squadron".
1779-09-20.en:
"I am to set out after to-morrow for ⟦— Texel,⟧ with Letters & secret Instructions to ⟦C[o]mmodore Jones [&] his squadron,⟧ whose arrival there I expect every day."

Holes, 2. As written, the numbers spell "csmmodore jones e his squadron" in both copies. C[o]mmodore: 12 = s, and the decipherer of item 93 image 260 wrote S over it; "Commodore" is certain by sense and agrees with the print (Wharton 3:333). [&]: 24 = e, and the decipherer wrote E; "&" supposes 241 with a figure dropped and is a guess; "Jones e his squadron" with a stray e is as possible.

1781-09-02.summary: "The city is Dort": the city whose resolution of 28 August on the French loan Dumas reports. Bare; the plain copy leaves it out.
1781-09-02.en:
"September 2d. A very interesting resolution of August 28th, of one of the principal cities of this Province, has been received the day before yesterday, by her Deputies here. ⟦The city is Dort.⟧ Of which the Substance is as following ..."

No emendation. 13 numbers, with no decipherer's letter over them.

system: Each number 1-682 is the position of a character in 13 printed lines of Dumas's 1775 preface to Vattel, Le Droit des gens; every occurrence of a letter is an alternative number for it.
